There were no schools, books, or teachers there.

core: The Fairy prepared a celebration for Pinocchio's transformation into a real boy.
Pinocchio went out to invite Lamp-Wick, his closest and laziest friend.
Lamp-Wick announced that he was leaving for the famous Land of Toys.
He described a country without schools, books, teachers, or any required work.
Pinocchio remembered the Fairy's promise, but endless play sounded irresistible.
At midnight, a crowded wagon arrived to carry the boys away.
The exhausted donkeys pulling it seemed to whisper warnings through their tears.
Pinocchio ignored every sign, squeezed aboard, and abandoned the waiting celebration.
In Toyland, children played from morning until night without correction.
Five carefree months passed without a single lesson or useful task.
Then Pinocchio awoke and discovered long donkey ears on his head.
A Marmot examined him and sadly diagnosed incurable Donkey Fever.
Pinocchio covered the ears and hurried to check on Lamp-Wick.
His friend was hiding the same ears beneath an oversized cap.
Laughter changed into braying as both boys became complete donkeys.
The wagon driver sold Pinocchio to a new owner and collected his profit.
studio: The Blue Fairy prepared the celebration that would mark Pinocchio's long-awaited transformation into a real boy.
Before the party, he went to invite Lamp-Wick, the companion most skilled at turning responsibility into a joke.
Lamp-Wick announced his departure for the Land of Toys, where vacation supposedly continued every day of the year.
No schools, books, teachers, schedules, or adult expectations disturbed the happiness he described.
Pinocchio defended his promise at first, yet the fantasy of unlimited amusement steadily weakened his resistance.
At midnight, a silent driver arrived with a wagon so crowded that the boys could barely find space.
The donkeys pulling it wept and whispered warnings, but their passengers heard only the destination.
Pinocchio climbed aboard, leaving the Fairy's prepared celebration and his almost-human future behind.
Toyland delivered exactly what had been advertised: noise, games, sweets, freedom, and no visible consequence.
For five months the children practiced nothing except amusement, while the hidden cost quietly developed.
One morning Pinocchio discovered that two long donkey ears had appeared where a boy's ears should be.
A solemn Marmot diagnosed Donkey Fever and explained that a life without learning produced this transformation.
Pinocchio hid the evidence beneath a cap and ran to Lamp-Wick, hoping the problem belonged to him alone.
His friend removed another oversized cap, revealing the same ears and the same terrified understanding.
Their nervous laughter became braying as hands, feet, voices, and bodies completed the change into donkeys.
The driver who had collected carefree children now sold the finished animals, turning false paradise into business.

core: A circus owner bought Donkey Pinocchio and trained him through punishment.
Soon the animal performed bows, dances, and dangerous jumps before crowds.
During one bright performance, Pinocchio recognized the Blue Fairy in the audience.
He tried to call her name, but his mouth produced only a donkey's bray.
Confused and distracted, Pinocchio missed a jump and injured one leg.
The circus owner immediately sold the lame donkey for almost nothing.
His next owner cared only about using the skin for a drumhead.
The man tied a heavy stone to Pinocchio and dropped him underwater.
Hungry fish consumed the donkey covering while the protected wooden body remained.
When the rope rose, the surprised buyer found a living marionette instead.
Pinocchio slipped free and explained that the Fairy had protected him.

studio: A circus owner purchased Donkey Pinocchio and converted the consequences of Toyland into a profitable performance.
Training replaced play with punishment until the animal could bow, dance, and leap through dangerous hoops.
During one glittering show, Pinocchio recognized the Blue Fairy watching from the crowded seats.
He attempted to call to her, but the human appeal emerged as nothing more than a humiliating bray.
Distracted by recognition and shame, Pinocchio missed a jump, fell heavily, and permanently injured one leg.
The owner who had valued his tricks sold the lame animal immediately for a handful of coins.
The second buyer saw no living creature at all, only a hide that could become a drumhead.
He fastened a stone to the donkey and lowered him into the sea to end the transaction efficiently.
Beneath the water, fish consumed the donkey covering while the Fairy's protection preserved the wooden marionette inside.
The rope returned not with a dead animal but with Pinocchio alive in his original wooden body.
He broke away from the astonished buyer, explaining that the Fairy had sent the fish to protect him.
As he swam through open water, an azure Goat called urgently from a white rock.
Relief lasted only until the Terrible Shark surfaced and opened a mouth large enough to resemble a cavern.
The rushing water defeated Pinocchio's strongest swimming and carried him directly toward the monster.
In a single motion the Shark swallowed him, replacing the open sea with complete darkness.
There Pinocchio met a resigned Tunny who had stopped believing that anyone could leave alive.

core: Pinocchio left the Tunny and followed a tiny light through the darkness.
At a small table, an old man ate beside his final candle.

Geppetto explained how the storm and Terrible Shark had swallowed him.
He had survived inside the monster for two long years.
Supplies from a swallowed merchant ship had provided food, candles, and matches.
Now the food was gone, and the candle on the table was the last.
Pinocchio insisted that they attempt an escape before darkness returned.
Although Geppetto could not swim, Pinocchio promised to carry him.
The ancient Shark's asthma forced it to sleep with its mouth open.
Their first attempt failed when a sudden sneeze threw them backward.
Pinocchio refused despair, took his father's hand, and climbed again.
At the final row of teeth, Geppetto climbed onto his son's back.
Pinocchio leaped into the moonlit water and began carrying them home.
studio: Leaving the resigned Tunny behind, Pinocchio followed a faint light through the vast darkness of the Shark.
The glow came from a final candle beside a tiny table where a white-haired old man ate live fish.
Recognition arrived almost too powerfully for speech: the prisoner was Geppetto, still waiting after two years.
Father and son embraced with the confused laughter and tears of people who had imagined each other lost.
Pinocchio released the entire journey in one breathless confession, naming temptations, lies, punishments, helpers, and regret.
Geppetto answered with his own story of the storm, the overturned boat, and the monster that swallowed him.
A merchant ship had also disappeared into the Shark, leaving enough supplies to sustain one man in darkness.
Those provisions had lasted two years, but now both the cupboard and the final candle were nearly empty.
Pinocchio immediately proposed escaping through the mouth, treating action as responsibility rather than impulse.
Geppetto admitted that he could not swim and doubted that a small marionette could carry him.
His son answered that they should test courage together rather than wait separately for the end.
Because age and asthma forced the Shark to sleep with its mouth open, moonlight marked a possible route.
A sudden sneeze destroyed their first attempt and sent them sliding back into darkness without the candle.
Pinocchio refused the language of defeat, found his father's hand, and led the climb a second time.
Beyond the tongue and three rows of teeth, Geppetto settled his weight onto the wooden shoulders.
Pinocchio leaped into the calm moonlit sea, finally using his strength to carry the father who had carried him.

studio: Pinocchio carried Geppetto toward the distant shore until exhaustion finally overcame his wooden strength.
The Tunny, inspired by their escape, arrived at the critical moment and carried father and son to safety.
Along the road, the ruined Fox and Cat begged from the victim whose trust they had once converted into profit.
Pinocchio recognized the consequence of their old deception, rejected their excuses, and calmly continued onward.
The Talking Cricket offered shelter in a straw cottage and reminded Pinocchio of the hammer thrown long ago.
Instead of defending himself, Pinocchio apologized, accepted the rebuke, and prepared a bed for his weakened father.
Farmer John offered one glass of milk in exchange for the exhausting labor of drawing one hundred buckets.
Every dawn Pinocchio returned to the well, transforming work into food and care for Geppetto.
In the stable he found Lamp-Wick dying as an overworked donkey, the final human cost of Toyland's promise.
For five months Pinocchio made baskets, studied by lamplight, and built a rolling chair for his recovering father.
His daily habits produced enough security for Geppetto and fifty saved pennies for a long-delayed new suit.
Before he could spend them, the Snail reported that the Blue Fairy lay ill without money for food.
Pinocchio surrendered every penny and chose to double his labor for the mother who had repeatedly rescued him.
That night the Fairy appeared in a dream, praising not perfection but the loving heart revealed through action.
He awoke in a renewed home as a living boy, while Geppetto stood healthy and young beside his workbench.
Looking at the abandoned wooden body, Pinocchio understood that becoming human had happened before his appearance changed.
